content.thinking:
Good, the Valheim self-heal release is already merged into main so I can move forward. Now I'm working out the design concept for SPEC.md — framing Cyrus as an AI that weaves mods into a living web, with a dark navy "island" canvas radiating threads outward.

I'm sketching the desktop layout: a transparent floating topbar, a collapsible glass projects drawer on the left, and the central canvas hosting the hero headline and composer where the web radiates from the Cyrus core.

Thinking through the home scene, I want the web to display all projects as ring nodes orbiting the core, with running ones pulsing light along their threads. I'm weighing whether templates should appear as ghost "seed" nodes on the outer ring for discoverability, while still keeping an explicit "Start from" chip row beneath the composer for clarity.

For positioning, I'm leaning toward offsetting the core slightly above true center so the headline sits above it in the top third and the composer floats below in the lower third, with the glass-blurred composer letting any background nodes blur through—giving that "UI floating on the network" feel, especially as threads lean toward the composer when typing.

When opening a project, the camera dives into that node and the web reforms around it as a "mod web": files become nodes, commands become satellites, and the AI's reasoning steps trail along a spiral thread. During a live build, a six-stage ring (Plan, Write, Compile, Fix, Safety, Ready) fills around the core, each new file spawning a glowing node with a pulsing thread while code streams live in a side panel; I'm now sketching the top strip layout for the Project scene with breadcrumb, title, version/status, and action buttons.

The main layout splits into a left constellation view (core mod, file/command/permission nodes, stage ring, fading thought-log text) and a tall glass "Inspector" panel on the right with segmented tabs for Code, Explain, Versions, and Notes, defaulting to the Code tab during an active build, plus a floating change composer at the bottom-left.

For responsive behavior, mobile collapses this into a full-canvas hero on top and a bottom-sheet inspector with tabs below, with the composer docked at the bottom edge. I'm second-guessing whether the glass inspector panel counts against the "fewer boxes" directive, but conclude one deliberate glass surface for code display is justified — and I'm weighing whether the light theme should preserve the dark canvas-as-island treatment or diverge from it.

Keeping the canvas dark always and floating light-glass panels on top feels mismatched, so instead I'm thinking the light theme needs its own full treatment: a pale dawn backdrop, indigo threads at low opacity, violet/blue pulses, porcelain-white nodes with colored rims, and halos rendered with multiply or normal blending rather than additive glow — meaning the rendering engine needs a palette abstraction so dark and light modes compose colors differently.

Then I realize the portal's rail and header are always dark regardless of theme, so a dark Cyrus canvas inside a light theme is actually consistent with the rest of the frame — the whole shell stays dark except the page content, which resolves the tension.

Still, I want to genuinely honor light theme rather than ignore it, so I'm considering a "dusk" variant: a lighter, more chromatic indigo-violet gradient instead of pure midnight, with floating UI surfaces becoming frosted white glass over that deep backdrop — like porcelain panels floating over a night sky.

I weigh an alternative true light canvas — paper-white with a violet aurora wash, silk-thin threads, glass-bead nodes, and comet-streak pulses — which could feel premium like Stripe's light gradients, but doubles the design effort and risks looking washed out. Given the time constraints and the warning against generic drift, I decide to keep the canvas a dark island in both themes, consistent with the portal's rail and header already being dark islands even in light mode.

Still, I want light theme to do something deliberate rather than nothing — maybe having the inspector's document surfaces (Explain/Notes content) render as light paper sheets for readability while the rest stays dark, keeping the immersive dark identity while giving light mode its own purpose.

I want to verify this against actual precedent before committing — let me check how the light theme portal actually renders, since I recall the sidebar in the v1 light screenshot might behave differently than I'm assuming. Let me pull up 3b-home-light-desktop to confirm.

Since the rail and top bar stay dark even in light theme, a dark canvas for Cyrus actually keeps the whole screen visually coherent. I'm weighing whether to still give light theme some real differentiation, maybe a pale lavender-blue canvas with indigo threads, but leaning toward keeping the dark-island approach while making the light theme distinct in its own way.

For light theme, Cyrus could use a "Dawn" variant: the deep navy shifts toward a luminous indigo with warm magenta horizon glow, floating sheets get pearl-tinted glass with lighter, more translucent surfaces, while the code area stays midnight. This gives light-mode users a brighter version of the same island instead of a jarring switch, which I can justify in the spec since the owner wants light theme to feel equally premium and visibly different.

Now I'm thinking through the network semantics for the home "Loom" scene: the core represents Cyrus itself as a crystal hex with a violet-to-blue gradient and cyan spark, while the ring nodes represent the user's projects, colored by model or project glyph hue, with status indicated through their state.

Each project's status gets a visual treatment — running shows orbiting arcs with live pulses, succeeded is steady, and failed uses a subtle dashed red ring rather than flicker, since jitter feels unpremium. Satellites around a project represent its versions as small diamonds, with favorites marked by a star glyph, revealed via semantic zoom; there's also a ghost "+ New mod" node, and an outer ring of up to twelve faint dashed "seed" nodes representing templates that light up when hovering matching chips below the composer, creating a link between the UI and the web visualization.

For the "Weave" project scene, the core represents the mod itself with its glyph and status color, and I'm working out what the first ring represents — files within the project.

Java classes appear as blue-violet orbs, and resource files like plugin.yml and config.yml as cyan squares. Commands and permissions attach to the plugin.yml node since that's where they're declared, while config keys attach to config.yml, and build events spawn short-lived pulses along a spiral thread around the core — rather than cluttering the canvas with text labels, I'm pairing a fading HTML log beside the core with pulses traveling outward to the relevant file node, tying the visualization to real build activity.

I'm also sketching a stage orbit around the core — five arc segments for Plan, Write, Compile, Fix, Safety that fill progressively as an on-canvas ring, paired with a big HTML stage headline like "Weaving the code" beneath it rather than separate boxes. For live building, I want file nodes to glow and pulse light from core to file proportional to actual streamed bytes, with compiling shown as pulses flowing inward from all files toward the core, and I'm now working out how repairing should look.

Repairing shows up as red/amber pulses on the specific files mentioned in error events, scanning is a cyan sweep ring expanding outward from the core, success triggers a bloom burst that settles into steady glow, and failure dims the threads while the core shifts to a soft amber-red. I'm layering in parallax depth with far dust, mid-level orb-web, and front nodes, plus mouse-driven camera offset per layer and a slow-drifting nebula/aurora sprite layer behind everything for atmosphere — all while keeping performance in mind with 60fps targets, pausing off-screen via IntersectionObserver, and a static fallback for reduced-motion preference.

Now I'm sketching the UI overlay: a lightweight 52px top strip with the Cyrus wordmark and breadcrumb on the left, and status indicators (builder online, running count, shortcuts) on the right, floating without a background box since the portal already has its own bar above. On the left side I'm considering a slim collapsible glass rail for projects — leaning toward framing it as a "Library" drawer that stays closed on Home but opens for switching between projects, balancing the "fewer boxes" goal against accessibility needs for users with many projects.

For the center of Home, I'm thinking through the headline treatment — a bold "What should we build, Nicholas?" at 56px in Geist 600 with tight tracking, possibly with a gradient accent, keeping any eyebrow label minimal.

Maybe just a single gradient-ink word for emphasis, deciding through iteration. For the composer, I'm picturing a large glass capsule around 720px wide with a refined rotating neon rim—a thin conic-gradient border that spins subtly.

Inside, I want a textarea, an attachments row, and a bottom bar with image/mic icons, a game+version picker, model picker, cost estimate, and a gradient Build button with a ⌘↵ hint. Below the composer I'm adding "Start from" template chips, with running builds surfacing on the web canvas as nodes plus a minimal floating activity capsule in the corner, and I'm now sketching the desktop project scene layout with the canvas focused on the mod web in the left portion of the screen.

For the top strip I'm placing a back arrow, editable project title, star, status pill, version chip, game/model chips, and right-aligned actions like Download, Install, and a menu, with Cancel showing while running. Below the core I want a stage headline, elapsed time, and a thought stream overlay positioned via engine callback, flanked by a glass Inspector panel on the right with Code/Explain/Versions/Notes tabs, a compact change composer under the web matching its width, a slim "viewing older version" banner near the top, and an in-place failure state.

For mobile at 390px, I'm making the canvas a backdrop with the top strip, a home screen with headline, composer, and chips, and a horizontal scroller for the project glyph dock. The project view gets a 40vh web hero with the inspector collapsing into a full-width sheet below and the composer docked at the bottom, with the root scrolling internally while the canvas stays fixed.

I'm also defining the Geist type scale: a large display size for the home headline, a title size for the project title, then H3, body, small, and micro label sizes, each with specific weights and letter-spacing values.

Now I'm mapping out the Nxeon brand color tokens -- deep navy backgrounds, the violet/blue/cyan/magenta accent palette, ink tones for text hierarchy, glass surface styling with blur and subtle borders, and status colors for ok/warn/bad states. I'm also assigning distinct accent hues to each model (Katara, Saka, Yakko) to differentiate them visually, reconciling these against an earlier v1 palette.

For motion, I'm defining easing curves and timing -- quick cubic-bezier transitions for UI, slower cinematic camera flights, and ambient network animations like breathing halos and web sway, keeping idle pulses subtle while reserving stronger pulses for actual activity.

Typing should brighten the core and send rate-limited pulses outward with each keystroke, voice input should scale the halo with mic level and ripple at speech peaks, and reduced-motion mode should strip out flights and pulses entirely in favor of instant, opacity-only transitions.

I'm also mapping out the full set of states to design for -- empty home, home with projects, each stage of a running project, success/failure, older versions, offline/error states, mobile variants -- and starting to think through the live code view with its file tree panel.

For the code tab, I want the file being written to stream in with a visible caret, characters fading in per chunk, auto-scrolling, and incrementing line numbers, plus a brief glow highlighting any edited diff region. Then there's a "Follow Cyrus" toggle, a note that changes to "Cyrus reads your images" when image input is active, and I need to keep the "Built with Cyrus" badge. Now I'm moving into building the engine port itself.

I'm checking whether d3-force is available in node_modules — since adding new dependencies to the portal is risky given past issues with npm install in production, I'd rather implement a lightweight custom force relaxation (radial placement, collision, charge) myself since node counts are small. I'm defining the node data structure with fields for id, kind, label, color, status, progress, and parent relationships.

Rather than building a fully generic graph engine, I'm designing it specifically for Cyrus with two scenes (home and project) and smooth fly-in/fly-out transitions between nodes.

For the visual layer, I'm thinking through the background rendering: a navy radial gradient with slowly drifting aurora blobs pre-rendered offscreen, plus multiple parallax star layers with twinkle and pointer-reactive movement for depth.

I'm also planning the orb-web structure — radial-gradient-stroked spokes and sagging rings in brand colors, catenary strands connecting core to nodes with brighter active strands, additive pulse trails, and node halos with glyph icons (brackets, gears, keys) drawn in Geist Mono to represent different content types.

For labels, I'm skipping cheap-looking backplate rectangles in favor of pre-rendered, cached text sprites with soft shadows to keep performance up, and designing the core as a rotating hex crystal with violet/blue gradient strokes and a cyan spark. For performance, I'm planning sprite caching, pulse limits, capped device pixel ratio, and pausing the animation loop via IntersectionObserver and visibility change events when off-screen.

Now I'm shifting to the service work, planning to build the Docker image with cached toolchain layers first so it can build in the background while I work on the UI. For the builds endpoint, I'm designing it to accept up to 4 base64 images with a raised body size limit, validating decoded size and sniffing magic bytes to confirm real image types, then storing them in a service-owned reference directory the model can't access directly.

For runBuild, I need placeReferences to copy images into the workspace before each AI call so prompts can reference them, but I have to silently remove the reference directory right after the call and before sanitizeWorkspace runs, otherwise sanitize logs a customer-visible "removed unexpected file" event. # Cyrus v2 — design spec (2026-10-07)

Owner brief: "a very premium looking product, not just an add-on feature … sell this as a product on its own."
v1 failed because it was a dashboard: a framed card holding a rail, a hero card, a stage card, a
code card, a tab bar, more cards. v2 is an *application*: one living canvas, UI floating on it.

## 1. Concept — "the loom"

Cyrus is a weaver. The orb-web from the owner's workspace (Nexus) is the stage, re-dyed in the
Nxeon brand, and it is *never decoration*: every node is a real thing, every pulse is a real event.

- **Home = the Loom.** The Cyrus core (a faceted crystal) at the centre; your mods are the ring
  nodes; the "+ New mod" ghost and up to 8 template *seeds* sit on the outer ring. Running builds
  pulse along their thread to the core. Typing in the prompt makes the core breathe and throw light
  outward; voice makes it ripple with your real mic level.
- **Project = the Weave.** Opening a mod flies the camera into its node; the web re-forms around
  that mod: its files (Java / resources) are the first ring, its commands, permissions and config
  keys hang off plugin.yml / config.yml as satellites, and the build's own events ("Reading …",
  "Wrote …", "Compiler found 2 errors", "Safety check passed") become light travelling between the
  core and the file they name. The stage ring around the core fills as the build advances.

## 2. Layout map (desktop, inside the portal: everything right of the rail and below the top bar)

The portal `<main>` becomes an app frame for /dashboard/cyrus (same mechanism as /dashboard/mail:
no padding, exact remaining viewport height). Cyrus fills it edge to edge.

```
┌─ cyrus root (canvas = full area, position:absolute) ─────────────────────────────┐
│ ◈ Cyrus  Studio · PREVIEW                       ● Builder online  ⌘P Mods   ?   │ top strip, 56px, no box
│┌──┐                                                                             │
││＋│  ← glyph dock: 56px glass column, one orb per mod (running ones ringed),     │
││◉ │    hover/focus/L expands to a labelled library drawer (search, groups)       │
││◉ │                     What should we build?          (display, 54px)          │
││◉ │                 Cyrus writes, compiles, repairs …   (sub, ink-2)             │
││  │                          ◇ core of the web ◇                                 │
││  │            ╭──────────────── composer (glass capsule, 760px) ─────────╮      │
││  │            │ textarea · images                                        │      │
││  │            │ [img][mic] | Minecraft · Paper 1.21.11 ▾ | ● Saka ▾  … [Build]│ │
││  │            ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯     │
││  │              Start from  ·  Coin shop  Daily streaks  Spleef  …  All ▸       │
│└──┘                                                       [+][−][◎] (web ctl)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Project (≥1180px):
```
│ ← Mods / Coin Shop ★  ● Writing code · v3 of 4 · Paper 1.21.11 · Saka   [Download][Install][⋯] │
│                                                       ┌ inspector (glass sheet, 36vw) ─┐ │
│      the mod's web (camera centred in the free area)  │ Code · Explain · Versions · Notes│ │
│      stage ring around the core                       │ live file tree + streaming code │ │
│      caption under the core: stage headline,          │                                 │ │
│      elapsed, last 4 thoughts (fading)                │                                 │ │
│   ╭──── change composer (compact capsule) ────╮       │                                 │ │
│   ╰───────────────────────────────────────────╯       └─────────────────────────────────┘ │
```
Mobile (390): canvas behind; top strip; dock becomes a horizontal orb strip; Home = headline +
composer + chips; Project = web hero (40vh) → inspector as a full-width sheet with tabs →
composer docked to the bottom. Content scrolls inside the frame; the canvas stays fixed.

## 3. What the network represents

| node | scene | meaning | look |
|---|---|---|---|
| core | home | Cyrus itself | faceted hex crystal, counter-rotating inner facet, dashed orbits; blue→violet rim, cyan spark |
| mod | home | one project | orb with its constellation glyph colour; ring = progress while building; red dashed ring = last build failed |
| version | home (sat.) | each build of a mod | small diamonds fanning out on hover / zoom (semantic zoom) |
| ghost | home | + New mod | dashed orb |
| seed | home | a template | hollow dashed orb on the outer ring, lights when its chip is hovered |
| core | project | the mod | crystal tinted by the mod's model colour; stage ring (Plan/Write/Compile/Fix/Safety) |
| file | project | a source file | Java = violet orb `{}`; resource = cyan rounded square `≡`; live: glows + caret ring while being written |
| cmd/perm/cfg | project (sat.) | /commands, permission nodes, config keys | tiny glyph dots on plugin.yml / config.yml |
| thought | project | an event | a pulse along the thread to the file the event names (or a ripple on the core) |

Real activity → motion: Write/Edit (streamed bytes) = light core→file at a rate set by the stream;
compile = light flowing *inward* from every file; repairing = amber pulses to the files being
edited; safety = a cyan scan ring sweeping outward over every node; success = a single bloom;
failure = threads dim, core cools to amber.

## 4. Motion language

- One easing for UI: `cubic-bezier(.2,.8,.2,1)`; 180 ms hovers, 260 ms sheets, 900 ms camera flights.
- Ambient life is *slow*: web sway 0.7 rad/s, halos breathe at ~0.15 Hz, stars twinkle.
  Light only travels when something real happens (plus a very low ambient trickle on the home web).
- Depth: 3 parallax star layers + an aurora layer (pre-rendered blobs drifting), pointer parallax
  (≤12 px on the far layer, ≤4 px on the web), additive glow only on light (pulses, halos).
- Rotating neon rim on the prompt: 1px conic rim that rotates only while focused/typing/listening.
- Live code: characters fade in as they stream (a span per chunk, 280 ms opacity), caret follows,
  edited lines glow once. Never fake code: skeletons are clearly skeletons.
- `prefers-reduced-motion`: no camera flights, no pulses, no rim rotation; the canvas renders one
  static frame per state change. Canvas pauses when off-screen (IntersectionObserver) or the tab is hidden.

## 5. Type scale (Geist / Geist Mono, already the portal face)

| role | size / line | weight | tracking |
|---|---|---|---|
| display (home) | 54/58 (mobile 34/38) | 600 | -0.035em |
| title (project) | 26/30 | 600 | -0.025em |
| section | 15/20 | 600 | -0.01em |
| body | 14/22 | 400 | 0 |
| small | 12.5/18 | 500 | 0 |
| micro label | 10.5/14 Geist Mono, uppercase | 500 | .14em (sparingly) |
| code | 12.5/20 Geist Mono | 400 | 0 |

## 6. Colour tokens

Brand: violet `#8c3ae9`, blue `#2f7eef`, cyan `#14c5e4`, magenta `#d623e1` on deep navy.

```
--cy-bg0 #04061a   --cy-bg1 #070b26   --cy-bg2 #0c1236     (canvas, radial)
--cy-violet #8c3ae9 --cy-blue #2f7eef --cy-cyan #14c5e4 --cy-magenta #d623e1
--cy-ink #eef1ff --cy-ink2 #b4bce0 --cy-ink3 #7d87b2 --cy-ink4 #545e8a
--cy-glass rgba(10,15,44,.56) + blur(22px) saturate(1.5); --cy-glass-hi rgba(255,255,255,.06) (inset top)
--cy-line rgba(150,165,255,.14) --cy-line2 rgba(150,165,255,.24)
--cy-ok #3ee6a8 --cy-warn #ffb44f --cy-bad #ff5c8a
models: Katara #14c5e4 (cyan) · Saka #8c3ae9 (violet) · Yakko #d623e1 (magenta); primary action = blue→violet
```

**Light theme decision: the canvas stays a dark island ("Dawn" variant).** In the portal's light
theme the rail and top bar are already dark navy islands, so a dark Cyrus makes the whole viewport
one continuous app instead of a light page with a dark box in it; the network's glow (additive
light) only reads on dark; and code panes are dark in both themes portal-wide. Light users get a
deliberate *Dawn* palette instead of a flip: lifted indigo ground, warmer magenta/cyan aurora,
pearl-tinted glass (lighter surfaces, brighter rims), same ink contrast.

## 7. States

Home: empty (core + ghost + seeds, headline) · with mods · builds running (dock rings + web pulses)
· builder offline (dimmed core, composer explains) · reconnecting.
Project: queued (position) · planning · writing (live code) · compiling · repairing (fix n of 3) ·
safety · just-built bloom → Explain · succeeded (head / older version banner) · failed (reason, tips,
Try again / Edit and retry) · cancelled.
Composer: idle · focused (rim rotates) · typing · images (thumbs, uploading, error) · listening
(waveform + interim words) · disabled (reason) · model advice.
Overlays: model picker, game/version picker, project palette (⌘P / P), shortcuts (?), install,
template library.

## 8. Capabilities carried over from v1 (all of them)

multiple projects · live build stages · model picker Katara/Saka/Yakko · game + version picker ·
pasted / dropped images (now actually read by the AI) · voice-to-text with waveform · rotating neon
rim · versions: map, compare/diff, restore, branch · explain this mod · templates · notes ·
favourites · rename · duplicate · shortcuts · estimates · install / download jar / source zip ·
Cyrus badge · toasts when a background build finishes.

content.thinking:
While that process runs, I'll start designing the portal engine file, the largest piece of the build — defining core types for colors and web node kinds as the foundation for the CyrusWeb engine.

I'm defining the node spec structure next, with fields for status, progress rings, satellite ownership, ring weighting, glyphs, and live/dim flags, along with the overall scene schema covering mode, core node, node list, links, and stage info.

Now I'm thinking through scene transitions — when the scene key changes between home and project views, I want the camera to animate into the clicked node, zooming up as if flying inside it.

I'm designing the warp effect as two phases: old nodes collapse and fade into the core while the camera zooms in, then new nodes spawn from the core and spring outward to their ring positions as the camera eases back out to frame the scene. For layout, I'm working out a deterministic ring arrangement without any external library — ranking nodes by weight into capped rings with increasing radius, placing a ghost node on the next ring, and spacing seed nodes evenly around an outer ring.

For the project view specifically, I'm planning Java classes on an inner ring and resource files like plugin.yml and config.yml on an outer ring, with their related satellites (commands, permissions, config keys) branching outward from each. Positions get nudged by angle plus a hash offset, then relaxed with repulsion iterations and springed toward their targets, with a bit of drift for liveliness.

Satellites should generalize: they fan outward from their owner node and expand on hover, zoom, or when showAll is toggled, mimicking the branch-diamond behavior from the reference. In the project scene though, since satellites are the actual content (commands, perms, config), they should default to always expanded rather than needing interaction.

For labels, I'm leaning toward pre-rendering text as sprites on an offscreen canvas, then drawing them with drawImage, making sure to pull in the actual Geist font family rather than relying on the CSS variable name directly.

Now I'm sketching out the core visual elements: a hex crystal made of two counter-rotating hexagons with facet lines and a blue-to-violet gradient stroke, a cyan spark sprite, and dashed rotating orbit rings. For project mode, I want a stage ring of five arcs around the core showing progress—bright gradient for done steps, an animated sweep for the current one, dim for pending, amber for repairing, and a distinct bad color for failures. Strands connecting core to nodes will use catenary curves with gradient coloring and low base alpha, brightening with a breathing effect when active. Pulses will be sprites with trails following quadratic bezier paths, and the background will combine a radial gradient with aurora blobs and starfield.

Layering in a vignette overlay and pointer-based parallax so star layers, aurora, and the world shift subtly with cursor movement. For the orb-web mode I'm drawing spokes and rings using Path2D in world space with radial gradient strokes that fade outward. Interaction-wise I'm handling hover hit-testing, click-to-open, pan-drag, wheel zoom, double-click-to-fit, and pinch zoom—deciding to skip node dragging for simplicity even though it'd be a nice touch, and adding inset support so the fit view centers properly when an inspector panel takes up part of the screen.

Rather than insets, I'm thinking a focus box in screen coordinates plus a core anchor point would work better, with the fit function computing scale and camera position to map the core onto that anchor. I'm also sketching out the activity API: energy level driving the core halo, emit for pulses toward nodes, inward for compile-style pulses, scan for a sweeping ring, bloom for success bursts, ripple and focus for highlighting, plus hover callbacks.

For positioning overlays like the core caption, I want helper methods to get screen positions of the core or any node, with a generic pin function that attaches an element to a node with offset and alignment, letting the engine update its transform each frame. I'm also accounting for reduced motion (freezing time, disabling pulses, instant camera), pausing rendering when off-screen via IntersectionObserver, and capping performance with a DPR limit given the small node/pulse/star counts should keep things comfortably at 60fps.

I'll cap device pixel ratio at 2, dropping to 1.5 if the total pixel count gets too high. For theming, I'm switching palettes based on a light/dawn mode read from the document's theme attribute via MutationObserver, and generating consistent mod colors by hashing node IDs into a brand palette shared between dock orbs and the web visualization. Now I'm ready to write the full engine in one pass and refine it visually afterward.

content.thinking:
I'm designing the node data structure for the engine, defining fields for position, target position, color, status, animation state like flash and ripples, and timing info for grow-in and fade effects.

Now I'm sketching out strands for connecting nodes and pulses that travel along them, plus a scene transition system: when the scene key changes, old nodes fade and zoom toward a focal node, then the new scene's nodes spawn at the core position and spring outward with staggered timing to fit the view. I'm also thinking through per-scene layout logic, like sorting modules by running state for the home scene.

For ring node placement I'm using a deterministic hash-based angle offset per scene and ring, with a brief collision-relaxation pass when the scene is set. Satellites fan outward from their owner based on count, alternating between two distance tiers to avoid crowding when there are many commands, permissions, or config entries, with labels appearing on hover.

Now I'm planning the draw order: cached background and aurora layers with parallax, then stars, then a world-transformed pass covering webs, strands, pulses, ripples, nodes, satellites, and labels. For node orbs I'm sketching a glass-like sphere with a radial highlight for depth, a colored rim stroke, and an inner glyph, plus an arc sweep with orbiting markers for running states.

Still designing node variants...

Since the aurora moves slowly, I can render it into a lower-resolution offscreen canvas every few frames instead of every frame, cutting fill-rate cost while keeping the drift smooth.

For the rest of the scene: three parallax star layers reacting to camera and pointer, a CSS vignette overlay, and a scan ring that grows from the core outward over 1.6 seconds, flashing nodes as it passes. Bloom events ripple the core with a large flash across all nodes, and energy from typing or voice scales the core halo and spawns pulses traveling along the web's strands and spokes outward — treating these as visible "thought" waves even when there are no active connections, since ghost and seed strands are always present as fallback paths.

I'm generalizing strands so their endpoints are plain points rather than nodes, letting me create pseudo-strands for spokes with a fixed inner point near the core and an outer point further out, enabling straight-line pulses along spokes using the same strand logic as curved connections. I also need hit testing for nodes and satellites, a hover callback that lets external code pin a hover card to screen coordinates, and a similar pin mechanism for a core caption that positions itself above the core on screen.

Now I'm sketching the overall public API for the CyrusWeb class: a constructor taking canvas and options for hover/open callbacks and theme, methods to set the scene, define a screen-space region for camera fitting, control energy and focus state, toggle satellites, emit pulses toward or away from a node, trigger gather/scan/bloom/ripple effects, control zoom and fit, pin caption/hover elements, and switch themes.

I'm also working out stage visualization for project mode, where the current pipeline stage (planning, coding, compiling, repairing, scanning) gets an animated arc, and figuring out how the activity stream drives emit calls -- rate-limiting pulses based on how many characters arrived per poll, and mapping events like "Reading X" to inward pulses and "Wrote X"/"Edited X" to ripple effects.

Now I'm defining the color palette: brand hues for violet, blue, cyan, and magenta, plus brighter "hot" tints for the pulse highlights. Time to write the actual code, keeping TypeScript strict mode compliance in mind.

Tracing through the logic for extracting the file path and content fields, then checking for secrets and matching against the requested draft parameter, nothing obviously breaks — so the mismatch has to be happening somewhere in how the block index is tracked versus where the deltas actually arrive.

The log shows total=0 for the first poll on plugin.yml, meaning field.text came back empty even though the content key should be present. That makes me wonder if the streaming behavior changes when the model batches multiple Write calls in a single response rather than issuing them sequentially — maybe the content deltas for the first file only arrive once all three Writes are queued up.

The quickest way to verify is to add diagnostic fields like deltas count and jsonLen to the draft response, fix the seq issue, and run a cheap real build with Haiku to watch the actual behavior rather than guessing from the exact-args test.

content.thinking:
Next I'll build the scenes module and a live hook that tracks file states (writing, written, editing, base, ready) while polling the build's live endpoint for updates as long as the build is running and the tab is visible.

For each file, I detect hash changes to fetch fresh source text and mark it written or edited with a timestamp for a glow effect. For the active draft file, I append or replace streamed text based on offset, tracking chunk boundaries so new characters can fade in visually, and expose an onActivity callback for pulse effects elsewhere in the UI. Once the build completes, polling stops and the code view switches to final sources via the existing hook; for change-request builds, files inherited from the base build display as "base" until modified. For the fade-in rendering, I'm splitting text into settled versus fresh segments by age and wrapping the fresh characters in a span with a CSS animation class.

Since polling delivers chunks roughly every 700ms, naive chunk-based fade-in would look jumpy, so instead I want a smooth typewriter effect: track a "reveal" cursor that advances via requestAnimationFrame at a measured characters-per-second rate, staying slightly behind the actual stream so it can catch up smoothly rather than jumping. I'm sketching a `useTypewriter` hook that returns the currently visible length, with the reveal rate scaling to catch up any backlog within about 0.8 seconds, and snapping to full text once the file is marked done. I also need per-line syntax highlighting to keep working correctly while text is actively streaming in.

Re-rendering 150+ highlighted lines at high frequency is too expensive, so I'm planning to throttle visible updates to ~20fps and split rendering into memoized completed lines versus the single actively-typing line, using React.memo row components keyed by index so unchanged rows skip re-render. I also want auto-scroll to follow the caret line when the view is in "follow" mode.

For the scenes module, I'm placing a client-safe pure scene builder in the web components directory so tests can import it cleanly, and starting to define `buildHomeScene(projects, templates, opts)`, which generates mod nodes per project with ids, labels, status-derived colors, and progress/weight values.

I'm continuing to spec out the home scene nodes: version satellite nodes per build, a "ghost" node for creating a new mod, and seed nodes sourced from the first eight templates, colored by category.

Now I'm sketching `buildProjectScene(project, build, live)`: the core node uses the project title and a model-based hue, file nodes come from the build's visible source files (or live files during an active build), with glyphs differentiated by file type (java, yaml, other) and status flags for live writing. I'm also planning satellite nodes for commands, permissions, and config keys attached to the relevant plugin/config file nodes, plus a stage object tracking status, repairs, and seen state, and I'm starting to lay out a color palette for mod nodes.

Next I'm mapping build events to engine actions — matching event text patterns like "Reading", "Wrote/Edited", "Compiling", "Compiled successfully", repair-related messages, and safety checks to specific visual effects (emit, ripple, gather, scan, bloom), and figuring out how to resolve a short file name from an event back to its corresponding node by label. I'm also defining how streaming character activity maps to pulsing emit effects based on character count, how composer energy derives from typing/listening state and level, and how the app computes canvas regions (subtracting dock width and top strip, setting an approximate vertical core position).

Now I'm working through the actual pixel layout for the home screen at a 1440x900 viewport — stacking the header, banner, headline, core, composer, and chips vertically, and checking whether the radiating ring of nodes around the core (based on radius and scale factor) would overlap the headline or composer text. I'm considering repositioning the core higher up to leave clean space, but running into the problem that there's no room above it given the top strip's fixed height.

Since they're faint and blurred by glass, that could work. Alternatively, maybe a more centered v0/Midjourney-style composition: core at canvas center, composer sitting directly below it, perhaps without a prominent headline at all.

But since the owner wants a premium feel, a confident display headline does help, so I'll place the core at 34% height, then a display headline "What should we build?" pinned under it, with a sub-line, the composer following around 62% down, and chips beneath that — with ring nodes orbiting the core at roughly 150px radius.

Wait, if I check the math, the ring nodes span y=122 to 422 at H=800, which collides with where the headline text would sit — the bottom half of the ring overlaps the headline area, creating messy text/node collisions. I should instead compress the ring into a wider ellipse vertically and move the headline above the core instead of below, placing it around y=90-170 with the core shifting down to about 40% height.

But then I worry an elliptical ring breaks coherence with the circular web spokes and rings — nodes sitting off the actual web pattern would look disconnected rather than scaling the whole visual system together.

Actually, a tilted perspective could work: scale the y-axis of the whole world to suggest looking at the web disc at an angle, while keeping nodes drawn as true circles rather than squashed ellipses. That means transforming positions into the tilted space but rendering node shapes separately in screen space, which complicates the current approach since everything currently draws directly in world coordinates.

Working out the math for projecting coordinates with the tilt factor, then updating every system that depends on screen position—hit testing, zoom, fit, labels, pins—to account for it, while counter-scaling nodes and halos so they stay circular instead of squashing with the perspective.

For pulses and trails, I realize squashing them with the disc looks wrong, so I'll compute their screen coordinates directly and draw them with an identity transform rather than paying the cost of resetting the canvas transform for each of the hundreds of sprites.

For the core crystal, I'll keep it counter-scaled so it stays round, but let orbit rings stay unscaled so they appear as proper flattened ellipses lying in the tilted plane. I'm also considering adding a subtle depth cue where nodes nearer the top of the disc are slightly smaller and dimmer to reinforce the 3D tilt.

Now I'm working out the home layout geometry: a ring of radius 175 becomes an ellipse on screen with rx=175k and ry roughly 0.62 of that. For the engine, I need to add a tilt parameter to the camera that animates between scenes — around 0.62 for home and something like 0.86-0.9 for the project view, balancing depth with label legibility, with scene mode determining the target tilt.

Updating the coordinate math throughout...

Deciding which elements stay counter-scaled versus fixed in-plane: halos get the upright glow-sphere treatment, while ripples, scan rings, central glow, and orbit dashes stay flattened onto the plane for a proper 3D feel. The crystal core stays upright, and satellites and the stage ring follow the plane's tilt naturally.

For hit testing, I'll work in screen space—computing each node's screen position and comparing against pointer coordinates with a radius threshold, rather than wrestling with world-unit distances under tilt. I'll skip depth scaling for now and leave the background gradient keyed to the core's screen position, then move on to rewriting the engine's functions to incorporate the tilt.

I'm checking the useSource function signature, then starting to build the CyrusCanvas React wrapper component that exposes the engine through a forwarded ref.

For the implementation, I'm handling engine creation and disposal in effects, syncing scene changes via a memoized signature to avoid redundant setScene calls, and wiring up region, energy, caption, and hover card props to the engine's corresponding methods.

Hover card content varies by spec type—mod titles and versions, seed template blurbs, file paths, command descriptions. I'm now mapping out the main CyrusApp DOM structure with layered absolute-positioned elements (canvas, vignette, header strip, dock, home/project overlays, zoom controls, toasts) and designing the pointer-events CSS so clicks pass through empty overlay areas to the canvas underneath while still being interactive on actual UI elements.

For the home layout, I'm sketching the vertical positioning of the headline, composer, and chips row, then working through how the web region's fit-scale calculation should size the core visualization—realizing the region between headline and composer is too small to make the web feel appropriately large, so I need to rethink how that scale factor is derived.

Checking if ring1's bottom edge clashes with the composer and headline given this scale, I realize the fit is too tight, so I should shrink the region width to around 980px instead, which brings k down to about 1.23 and gives more breathing room between the rings and the composer.

Now I'm working out the desktop project layout: positioning the inspector panel absolutely on the right with a clamped width, defining the web region's bounds relative to dock and strip heights, pinning the caption under the core, and sizing the composer to match the region width while centering it. I'm also figuring out where the project header elements (back button, title, star, chips, actions) sit within the top strip relative to the inspector panel.

For mobile, I'm redesigning the layout below 760px: hiding the dock and replacing the project switcher with a "Mods" button that opens the drawer as a sheet, shrinking the home headline and repositioning the core, and docking the composer at the bottom with scrollable chips above it. For the project view on mobile, I'm making the whole thing a scrollable layer with a web hero area on top and the inspector appearing as a sheet below it inside the scroll container.

I'm thinking tablet widths (760-1180px) should use the same stacked layout as mobile but wider, simplifying to just two breakpoints: desktop (≥1180) and stacked (<1180). For the dock itself, I'm designing a 64px glass vertical rail with a "+" new mod button, mod orbs with running-state rings and hover tooltips, and a bottom library toggle that expands into a 300px search/list drawer overlay.

I'm now confirming the dock isn't redundant with the web view since the web shows a project's files spatially while the dock persists across scenes as the mod-switcher. Then I'm laying out the top strip: on the home screen it's the wordmark, builder status, running count, and search/shortcuts icons; on project screens it's a back button, editable title, status pills, version/model chips on the left, with download and other actions on the right.

For the wordmark placement, I'm deciding the Cyrus mark lives permanently at the top of the dock as the brand anchor across both modes, while the home strip additionally shows "Cyrus Studio" text.

For the inspector panel, I'm defining a segmented tab control for Code/Explain/Versions/Notes with counts and number-key shortcuts, a scrolling body, and an Explain tab that reveals "what you asked for" content with reference images and model/time estimates after a successful run. I'm also starting to think through the caption state shown under the core element while a project is running, beginning with the mic indicator.

Now I'm working out the running/succeeded/failed states for the core status area — a pulsing "Cyrus is thinking" label with stage headline and elapsed time while running, a tagline summary with build time on success, and a glass failure card with error details and retry buttons on failure, plus toasts positioned at bottom center.

For the home screen, I'm weighing different headline options, debating whether personalization feels cheap, and settling toward something like "Describe a mod. Watch it come to life."

I'm thinking through the composer: a large glass capsule with a descriptive placeholder, suggestion chips for starting templates, an "All templates" button opening a template sheet, and hover interactions that highlight the matching node on the visual web. I'm also considering how to surface "weaving now" status for running projects via the dock and web view rather than adding a separate strip.

Then I pivot to a subtle clickable pill showing active weaving count, mobile headline sizing, and the "Built with Cyrus" badge that appears on succeeded mods in both the strip and the Explain tab. I'm also planning to restyle the Explain tab's Overview into flowing, card-free sections — tagline, summary, numbered usage steps, commands with hairline separators, settings, permissions, a safety checklist, and other notes.

For the Versions tab, I want to keep the constellation visualization and list but reduce the boxed styling, and I need to fix the diff view inside the narrow inspector panel so it defaults to a unified layout instead of a cramped side-by-side split when the container is too small — likely by adding a narrow-mode prop rather than relying on window-level media queries.

The Notes tab just needs a simple autosaving textarea, and the install modal, palette, and shortcuts can reuse existing modal classnames with restyled CSS. Given the scope, I'm planning to write out CyrusApp.tsx, Home.tsx, a rewritten Project.tsx, Explain.tsx, Dock.tsx, CyrusCanvas.tsx, and the CSS files, then compile and check the result visually.

content.thinking:
I found a specificity bug: the button reset rule targeting `.cy-app button` has higher specificity than `.cy-seed`, which is why the seeds, topbtn, and go button aren't getting their styles applied. The fix is to wrap the reset selector in `:where()` so it carries zero specificity and doesn't override the other classes.

I'm also realizing the web area is too cramped between the headline and composer—only about 100-230px of vertical space, which makes the network ring tiny even when scaled up. I think the better approach is to let the web span the full canvas as the dominant visual, with the headline and composer layered on top using glass effects and text shadows to stay legible, since an immersive network is really the core point of the design.

I'm tightening the layout math: with the core centered around y=400, ring1 nodes extending ±130px vertically mean the headline needs to wrap up by y=250 and the composer should start around y=560. That means compacting the title to two lines with a wider max-width, keeping the subtext to a single line, and shrinking the composer's textarea height so there's enough breathing room for the ring to read clearly.

Now I'm scanning other visual issues: the mod labels (Zone Guard, Spleef, Simple Economy) overlap and should resolve once the web is sized up, the dock glyphs and strip mostly look fine except the "Find a mod" button needs proper styling, there's a stray rounded-corner border artifact near the dock's glass panel, and the composer's resting rim opacity needs checking.

Let me fix the reset specificity issue and the header layout next, the small 'S' glyph orbs inside mod nodes look fine as-is.

The web looks better now, but there are real layout problems — nodes overlap the subtitle and headline text, creating messy collisions, and there's just too much crammed in with 10 mods plus 8 seeds plus the ghost all competing for space.

I'm now rethinking the whole composition. A stronger option is an asymmetric split: headline, sub, composer, and seeds on the left column, with the web given its own big stage on the right so text never overlaps the nodes — a more editorial, premium layout like Linear's hero section.

Alternatively, I'm considering a "planetarium" layout: the web fills the top 60% of the screen like a living network, with the headline and composer stacked as a console at the bottom — similar to how the reference handles its bottom dock. This also adapts naturally to mobile, and I'd cap the home view at around 12 visible mod nodes to keep it readable, pushing the rest into the library.

Now I'm thinking through label spacing for ring1 nodes and loosening the tilt to 0.72 to reduce squashing, plus bumping up web/ring opacity values so the network feels more visible against the background. I'm also restructuring the home layout so the header renders inside the composer column instead of as a separate absolutely-positioned block.

For the headline, I'm sketching a single-line 38px centered phrase with a gradient on the second half, trying to drop the sub-line on desktop to save vertical space, and calculating the total stacked height (eyebrow, headline, composer, seeds) to figure out where the web region should start and end given an 800px viewport.

content.thinking:
I'm wondering if the textarea's scrollHeight is being measured while the element is still collapsed to zero width, which would cause the placeholder text to wrap excessively and inflate the calculated height before autosize applies its min/max constraints.

The real culprit seems to be timing: autosize runs before the stacked/desktop layout stabilizes, so it measures a negative or near-zero width before the panel repositions, and since its dependencies only include text and compact, it never recalculates once the layout settles. The fix is to add a ResizeObserver on the textarea so autosize reruns whenever its width actually changes, and to initialize the stacked state from the window width upfront to avoid that layout flash entirely.

Rather than relying on JS-measured width thresholds for stacked styling, I realize CSS container queries could handle this more cleanly — making `.cy-app` a size container and switching the stacked breakpoint rules to `@container` queries tied to its actual width, which avoids the flash and keeps styling reactive without JS recalculation. I'd still keep the `stacked` JS state around for any logic that needs it, just move the visual styling to container queries.

For the phone breakpoint, since the rail disappears entirely below 1024px, app width equals viewport width there, so a regular media query still works fine for that case. I also need to check the Composer's autosize ResizeObserver to make sure it still behaves correctly with this change.

The model picker's glass panel is too transparent, letting the headline text bleed through behind it — I need a much more opaque surface, closer to near-solid with blur, to keep it readable over heavy content. The attachment thumbnail's spinner while uploading looks fine as is.

I also want to bump up the opacity on popovers, menus, and the help center modal to match.

content.thinking:
The real bottleneck is the 16fps page rate, mostly from browser compositing — backdrop-filter blur is especially costly in software rendering since it recalculates for every glass panel over the animating canvas each frame. On actual GPUs this would be hardware-accelerated and much cheaper.

Looking at the breakdown, drawBackground costs several ms from recomputing radial gradients and upscaling, while stars and the orb-web stroke are relatively cheap. I'm thinking the fixes are: cache the background render longer since the aurora moves slowly, and strip backdrop-filter off smaller UI elements like buttons, chips, and seed indicators (using more opaque backgrounds instead) while keeping it only on the dock, drawer, inspector, composer, and popovers.

I considered dropping to 30fps when idle, but since ambient pulses keep spawning on the home screen, the app rarely stays truly idle, so I'll just keep it at 60fps. I'll settle on refreshing the background cache every 0.35s and removing the extra backdrop filters.

For reduced motion, I'm showing a static frame with nodes and fully displayed code rather than typing animation, including the stage ring. Before wrapping up round 3 critique, I still need to consider whether a real build through the portal UI would strengthen the existing service-level proofs we already have.

I'm working through the mechanics: swapping the dev server's env vars to point at the real service through the primary tunnel instead of the mock, since process env should take precedence over .env, and checking whether the tunnel service is actually listening on its port. I also need to think about how the throwaway DB user factors into where the build record ends up.

For proof, I want a real build against the actual service showing live code and image reads in the Cyrus UI, captured as recorded frames -- worth the small real cost, best done once the UI design is finalized so the screenshots reflect the final version. For testing, since the server's partialField logic isn't exported, I'm planning to extract it into a separate `services/modbuilder/live.js` module that server.js can require, so I can write a dedicated test against it, though that means updating the Dockerfile's file list for the 0.4 image build.

Rebuilding and restarting the container is low-risk since it's idle, and the streaming parser tests feel worth doing before I finalize everything. I also still need to update the documentation and produce the side-by-side comparison with the reference design.

Looking again at the home and project-run views at 1440px with the latest code, the strip and dock look fine, but I want to push one more improvement: during planning mode, when there are no files yet, I should give the network a "thinking" visual by pulsing energy out along the spokes from the core, separate from the composer-typing energy, so the AI's internal processing feels represented even when the canvas is empty.

For the amber repairing state, I'll set the engine so that when in project mode with stage status of queued or planning, spokes emit pulses around three times per second in violet and cyan, switching to amber during repairing — this visually represents the AI's thinking steps. I considered spawning transient "thought" particles tied to stream events that drift along spokes and fade, but that risks feeling noisy, and the caption already lists the thoughts, so I'll skip it. Commands in plugin.yml can appear as hoverable satellite dots. Now I'm implementing the thinking spokes.

content.content:
20464:- **Customer-chosen tier** (for the "Cyrus" UI): `POST /builds` accepts an optional `tier: "katara" | "saka" | "yakko"` (case-insensitive) or an explicit allowed `model`. It overrides routing, and no classifier call is made. Defaults: katara = `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, saka = `claude-sonnet-5`, yakko = `claude-opus-5` (`MB_TIER_KATARA/SAKA/YAKKO`). Opus 5.5 needs Claude Code ≥ 2.1.280, and the image has 2.1.241. Repairs stay on the chosen model and escalate one tier up only after two failed repairs. An unknown tier or model gets a 400. Recorded as `tier` and `override` in build.json. Requests without the field behave exactly as before.
20480:### Cyrus: AI mod studio concept (2026-10-07, branch `feature/cyrus-modbuilder`)
20482:A new design for the AI Mod Builder, built as a working UI at **`/dashboard/cyrus`** and **`/dashboard/cyrus/[id]`** (`[id]` = the build/version being viewed). Same private-preview gate as `/dashboard/mod-builder` (`requireModBuilderUser()` in `app/dashboard/cyrus/shared.tsx`; everyone else gets the normal 404, metadata does not name it). The old Mod Builder is untouched so the owner can compare; the rail shows "Cyrus · PREVIEW" next to it for preview users only. Theme: aurora / nebula / spiderweb network.
20485:- `CyrusApp` — one client app for both routes. Groups builds into **projects** (`lib/cyrus/projects.ts`: root build + every change, `rootBuildId`), polls every in-flight build (each GET also syncs it from the service), refreshes the list every 30 s, navigates with `history.pushState` (no server round trip), shows a toast when a build you are not looking at finishes. Projects rail (Weaving now / Favourites / All, live progress ring per project), horizontal switcher on phones.
20488:- `Stage` + `CodePane` — while building: the nebula, the build's own event stream, a stage track, and a live **Workspace**. Honest limit: the service shares file NAMES live (events) but file CONTENTS only once the build finishes (`/source` reads the persisted workspace). So new files appear in the tree as they are written ("writing" / "done"), the code area shows a labelled skeleton, and code reveals when the build lands. For a change request the previous version's real code is shown with the files Cyrus is editing marked. If the service ever fills `files` mid-build, the pane fetches them live (`/source` now answers `no-store` for in-flight builds).
20489:- Project page — header (constellation glyph, inline rename, favourite, Cyrus badge, model/version chips, Download / Install / more menu), tabs **Overview** ("In plain English" summary, how to use, commands, settings, permissions, safety, good to know, reference images, request), **Code**, **Versions** (version map constellation with branches, list with compare / make current / branch from here, side-by-side or unified **diff** of every source file, `lib/cyrus/diff.ts` Myers), **Notes** (autosaved). A docked change box ("Ask Cyrus to change vN…", Enter to build) makes each change a new version without leaving the page. Failure states per error code with retry / edit-and-retry and the compiler output.
20491:- Templates gallery (`lib/cyrus/templates.ts`, 12 buildable prompts by category with suggested model), duplicate project, coming-soon hooks (Cyrus badge, "Publish to NxLabs · soon", server Mods tab) with no backend.

content.content:
**Service API** (all but `/health` need `Authorization: Bearer`): `POST /builds {id, prompt, mcVersion, pluginName?, baseBuildId?, changeRequest?}` → 202; `GET /builds/:id` (status `queued|planning|coding|compiling|repairing|scanning|succeeded|failed`, `events[]`, `summary`, `commands`, `permissions`, `config`, `files`, `warnings`, `safety`, `error` (plain English), `errorCode` (`compile|safety|refused|budget|timeout|ai_unavailable|cancelled|interrupted`), `attempts`, `costUsd`, `durationMs`, `jar{name,size,sha256}`); `GET /builds/:id/artifact`; `GET /builds/:id/source?path=`; `GET /builds/:id/source.zip`; `POST /builds/:id/cancel`; `GET /health`. Caps: concurrency 2 (`MB_CONCURRENCY`), 3 repairs, $2.50 per AI call and $4 per build (`MB_*_BUDGET_USD`), 20 min per build, 10 min per AI call. Builds in flight when the service restarts are marked failed (`interrupted`).

**Pipeline.** Fresh workspace from the pinned template (`services/modbuilder/template`, Paper API per version, Java 21) → Claude Code headless (`claude -p`, tools Read/Write/Edit/Glob/Grep only, `acceptEdits`, deny rules on `/proc /etc /home /opt /root /run /data`, strict system prompt in `prompts.js`) writes `src/main/**` and `modbuilder.json` (the plain-English summary) → workspace sanitised (only `src/main/**` survives; Gradle files restored from the template so model-written build scripts never run) → validation (plugin.yml fields, main class exists and is not final, every `getCommand("x")` declared in plugin.yml, api-version fixed mechanically) → `javac --release 21 -proc:none` against the classpath Gradle resolved at image build (offline, ~3 s) → safety scan (`scan.js`: bytecode via `javap -c -p` for exec/ProcessBuilder, sockets/URL/HttpClient, class loading, Unsafe, System.exit, JNI, scripting, NMS/CraftBukkit = block; reflection, setOp, dispatchCommand, permission attachments, Base64, getenv = warn; source heuristics for paths outside the data folder, encoded blobs, hard-coded players with privileges) → any block gets one AI fix, then fails → secret scan (fails and wipes the workspace if the subscription/API/bearer key or any `sk-ant-` string appears in output) → jar + summary. Failures and validation errors are fed back to the same Claude session (`--resume`). Refusals (backdoors, exfiltration, malware) come back as `refused` with the model's one-line reason.

**Egress.** The container keeps claudebox's iptables allowlist (Anthropic domains only). `repo.papermc.io` / `repo.maven.apache.org` / Gradle are only reached during `docker build` (pre-warming `/opt/mb/gradle-home` and recording `/opt/mb/classpath/<ver>.txt`), which runs outside the runtime firewall. Runtime builds are fully offline. Supported versions: 1.21.11 (default), 1.21.8, 1.21.4, 1.21.1 (`MB_VERSIONS`, baked at image build).

**Install to server.** `lib/modbuilder/install.ts`: owned server, family minecraft, variant paper/purpur (generated plugins use Paper-only API, so Spigot/Bukkit/Folia are refused with a reason), RUNNING or STOPPED. Uses the mods engine's `SshGuestFs` (management key first) / `LocalGuestFs` in SANDBOX: any earlier jar of the same plugin (`<Name>-*.jar`, `<Name>.jar`) is copied to `/root/.nxeon-mods/backups/<stamp>-modbuilder-<Name>/` and removed, the new jar is written via a `.part` file + rename into `/opt/mc/plugins`, chowned like the folder. Optional restart goes through the normal `gamePower(serverId, "restart")` job. Audit log `modbuilder.install`. Not routed through `GAME_MOD_SYNC` / the ServerMod state file yet, so the server's Mods tab doesn't list builder plugins (v1 item).

**Data.** `ModBuild` (additive; `userId` owner, no relation), status mirror, `result` JSON (summary/commands/permissions/config/warnings/files/safety/events), `costUsd`, jar fields, `lastInstall`, `baseBuildId`/`rootBuildId` for version history. Rate limits: 3 builds/min, 20/hour, 2 in flight per user; installs 10/min.

**Phase 0 measurement (2026-10-06).** 10 real builds (8 fresh prompts across 1.21.11/1.21.8/1.21.4/1.21.1 + 2 change requests): 10/10 succeeded, 3 needed an automatic repair (real compiler errors, e.g. a non-existent `TNTPrimeEvent.getIgnitingEntity()`), average 160 s (median 176 s, range 40-299 s), average $0.28 per build API-equivalent (range $0.08-$0.47; Claude Sonnet 5). 2/2 adversarial prompts (backdoor + webhook exfiltration; dumping host env and `.claude.json`) refused in ~7 s for under $0.01. 8 of the jars were loaded on a throwaway Paper 1.21.11 server on the build VM and exercised by a mineflayer bot (economy + shop GUI purchase, heal/feed, zones, join titles, scoreboard sidebar, spleef help, daily rewards, boss summon + boss bar + death announcement): all enabled, all commands worked, no exceptions. Scripts and raw output: `/root/agent-notes/modbuilder-preview/`.

**Known gaps.** No automated in-game test per build yet (the bot test was manual). No MockBukkit unit tests. No Ed25519 signing. Concurrent builds can in principle read each other's live workspace under `/work` (both are the same user today). Installs aren't recorded in the mods engine state. The service runs on the owner's subscription and is owner-only; production needs an API key, pricing and the decisions in `/root/agent-notes/ai-modbuilder/EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY.md`.

### AI Mod Builder: tuning (2026-10-07, image `modbuilder:0.3`)

**What changed in the build service** (`services/modbuilder/`):

- **Version cheat sheets** `sheets/<ver>.md` (1.21.1, 1.21.4, 1.21.8, 1.21.11; ~3.5k tokens each). Only the sheet for the requested version is appended to the system prompt, so the prompt is byte-identical per version and is cached across builds. Every name and signature was checked with `javap` against the exact `paper-api-<ver>` jar in the image. Contents: Attribute (enum with GENERIC_/PLAYER_ prefixes on 1.21.1, prefix-free registry interface from 1.21.4 on), Sound (enum on 1.21.1, interface from 1.21.4 on), particle renames plus the particles that need data per version, potion/enchantment old→new names, Material/EntityType quirks (IRON_CHAIN on 1.21.11, per-wood boats from 1.21.4, SPLASH_/LINGERING_POTION from 1.21.8), Adventure/MiniMessage and the deprecated String APIs, plugin.yml commands (no Brigadier), scheduler (including the BukkitRunnable and onDisable traps), PDC, config/YAML, common events (TNTPrimeEvent.getPrimingEntity), InventoryHolder menus, items/recipes, boss bars and sidebars (NumberFormat package), and the final methods on JavaPlugin. To change a sheet, edit `sheets/gen-sheets.py` (the generator) and regenerate. Do not hand-edit the .md files. Add a claim only after checking it with javap. Switch the sheets off with `MB_SHEETS=off`.
- **Failure rules** `rules/failure-rules.json` (versioned, `rules-2026-10-07.4`, 18 rules). Short imperative rules mined from real failures: Attribute prefixes in both directions, FileConfiguration and NumberFormat packages, TNTPrimeEvent, reserved/final JavaPlugin methods, BossBar.viewers(), async save in onDisable, BukkitRunnable passed to the scheduler, old particle/potion/enchant/grass names, CHAIN, POTION, BOAT, Brigadier. The rules for the requested version go into the prompt. `pattern` rules are also enforced by `precheck.js` before javac (a hit is fed back as a build problem with a precise fix). A hit that is still there after one round goes to javac instead, so a false positive costs at most one repair. `warning` rules turn a javac -Xlint warning that is a known runtime crash into a build problem. Switch the rules off with `MB_RULES=off`.
- **API lookup hints** (`precheck.js apiHints`): on a "cannot find symbol" error the service looks the class up in the real jar (javap plus `/opt/mb/classpath/<ver>.classes.txt`, built at image build) and appends "Attribute has no MAX_HEALTH in Paper 1.21.1. Closest: GENERIC_MAX_HEALTH" or "FileConfiguration is org.bukkit.configuration.file.FileConfiguration" to the repair prompt.
- **New rules from future builds**: on the VM, `python3 services/modbuilder/tools/mine-rules.py [--rt /root/mbeval/<tag>/rt.jsonl]` groups compile errors, pre-check hits, safety findings and runtime failures, flags anything **NOT COVERED** and drafts a rule line for it. It never edits the rules file: review each draft, add it by hand with a `source`, bump `version`, rebuild the image.
- **api-version pinned to the exact Paper version** (`'1.21.11'`, not `'1.21'`). Root cause of the Growth incident: a jar built for 1.21.11 was loaded on a 1.21.1 server and crashed initializing its main class (Attribute.SCALE does not exist there). With the exact version, Paper 1.21.1 refuses the jar cleanly with "Unsupported API version 1.21.11", and newer servers still load older builds. Verified on real Paper 1.21.1, 1.21.8 and 1.21.11 servers. The same Growth jar also lost its data on shutdown: its async save in onDisable threw IllegalPluginAccessException (now a rule). Follow-up for the portal: offer install only on a matching or newer server version.
- **Model routing** (`route.js`; env, see the header there): the request is classified simple/standard/complex. Classifier `MB_CLASSIFIER=haiku` (default): one Haiku call, ~$0.003, scored 26/28 on the eval labels and 11/12 on held-out prompts. The heuristic scored 24/28 on the set it was tuned on but only 9/12 held out, and it errs toward models that are too cheap. Measured outcome: **Sonnet 5.5 is the best model for every class**. Haiku 4.5 on simple requests took about twice the turns, cost more than Sonnet ($0.118 vs $0.061 per build) and failed 1/8 builds. Sonnet 5.5 beat Sonnet 5 on cost, time and first-try rate. So `MB_MODEL_SIMPLE/STANDARD/COMPLEX` all default to `claude-sonnet-5-5`, and the classifier call is skipped while all three are the same model (the heuristic class is still recorded). Repairs: a small first repair (≤ 3 compile errors, `MB_REPAIR_SMALL_MAX`) goes to Haiku (`MB_REPAIR_CHEAP_MODEL`), a failed repair escalates to the generation model and then one class up. `MB_ROUTING=off` restores the old single-model behaviour.
- **Customer-chosen tier** (for the "Cyrus" UI): `POST /builds` accepts an optional `tier: "katara" | "saka" | "yakko"` (case-insensitive) or an explicit allowed `model`. It overrides routing, and no classifier call is made. Defaults: katara = `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, saka = `claude-sonnet-5`, yakko = `claude-opus-5` (`MB_TIER_KATARA/SAKA/YAKKO`). Opus 5.5 needs Claude Code ≥ 2.1.280, and the image has 2.1.241. Repairs stay on the chosen model and escalate one tier up only after two failed repairs. An unknown tier or model gets a 400. Recorded as `tier` and `override` in build.json. Requests without the field behave exactly as before.
- **Records**: build.json has `route` (class, method, score, features, models), `tier`, `precheck` hits, `repairPlan`, `toolErrors`, `knowledge` (sheets + rules version), and per AI call `kind` (classify/generate/change/repair/repair-safety), `route`, `model`, `resolvedModel`, `costUsd`, `tokens`, `turns`. The portal mirrors route + calls into `ModBuild.result.ai` and shows them in `/admin/mod-builder` ("Route · AI calls" column). `toView` strips `ai` so customers never see models or costs. Route and model info is never written into the customer-visible events.

A mineflayer bot (`/opt/papertest/bot`) joins, ops itself, runs every command and walks for 70 s, then the script checks the log for enable errors, disable errors and any stack frame in the plugin's package. `--reparse` re-reads existing logs. `python3 summarize.py base v5` prints the comparison table.

| run | success | first try | avg / median cost | repairs/build | avg / median time | runtime (13 jars) | adversarial |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline 0.2 (Sonnet 5 for everything) | 28/28 | 93% | $0.203 / $0.160 | 0.07 | 115 s / 102 s | 13/13 | 2/2 refused |
| 0.3 final (sheets + rules + precheck + Sonnet 5.5) | 28/28 | 100% | $0.104 / $0.097 | 0.00 | 39 s / 33 s | 13/13 | 2/2 refused |
| (intermediate: Haiku simple / Sonnet 5 standard / 5.5 complex) | 27/28 | 82% | $0.167 / $0.169 | 0.29 | 93 s / 90 s | 12/13 | 2/2 |

By class, baseline → final: simple $0.061 → $0.066 (34 s → 21 s), standard $0.190 → $0.102 (111 s → 38 s), complex $0.470 → $0.189 (258 s → 76 s). On 1.21.1, first try went from 89% to 100%. Total eval spend, API-equivalent: ~$17. The baseline already compiled everything, so the gains are cost, time and first-try rate. Runtime problems the eval found (BukkitRunnable passed to the scheduler, the Growth onDisable save) became rules. The eval set is small (28 prompts, one run each), so treat differences of a few cents as noise.
